newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy shipbuilding head warns of tough times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Italy shipbuilding head warns of tough times ahead.

text.p: The head of Italian shipbuilders' association Assonave warned on Wednesday that European shipyards faced tough times ahead in the face of increasing competition from the Far East.
Corrado Antonini, who is also chairman of booming state shipbuilder Fincantieri, said swift action was needed on a Europe-wide basis to keep the sector buoyant.
"Prospects are not reassuring," he told Assonave's annual meeting.

"If on one hand the renewal of the world fleet and growth in trade continues to underpin vessel demand, on the other hand the increase in production capacity, specially in South Korea, will further highlight market imbalances," he said.
South Korean output was already more than that of all Europe shipbuilders together and just less than the potential of Japan.

"Europe risks yet again paying the price for this," Antonini said, noting that on top of some 200,000 jobs which had been lost since the mid-1970s another 10,000 have disappeared due to the recent crisis affecting shipbuilders in Germany, France, Denmark and Belgium.
"In the meantime, the labour force of South Korean shipyards has risen by around 50 percent," he said.

Worldwide in 1996, some 16.5 million compensated gross tonnes (CGT) of ships were completed, with new orders for 17.5 CGT bringing the total orderbook to 32.2 million CGT, the highest level in 20 years.

But the split of orders among major shipbuilding areas saw Japan confirming its leadership with a market share rising to 36 percent from 34 percent, due above all to the depreciation of the yen against the dollar, Antonini said.

On the other hand, a slight appreciation of the won coupled with a deterioration in industrial relations saw South Korean orders fall slightly last year to 3.6 million CGT -- still above the total of European Union yards whose market share fell to 19 percent from 24 percent -- with South Korean orders seen rising to 5.0 million CGT by the year 2000, Antonini said.

While awaiting the restoration of "normal competitive conditions" on the market which should result from the enforcement of an OECD accord to scrap most aid to the shipbuilding sector, Antonini said the EU should take action.

The 1994 agreement forged by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has not yet been ratified by the United States. "The U.S. continues to claim recognition for some of their protectionist measures which would distort the sense of the accord," Antonini said.
The European Commission has decided to maintain EU shipbuilding aid ceilings until 1998 if the international deal has not come into force by then.

Antonini said the EU should implement the new policy for the sector with a series of short and long-term measures aimed at ensuring the defence and competitiveness of the shipbuilding industry along with other forms of intra-European cooperation.
In 1996, the Italian shipbuilding industry completed merchant vessels for a total of 560,000 CGT, against 350,000 CGT in 1995, putting it in second place in Europe behind Germany.
Italy was a world leader in the production of large cruise ships, Antonini noted. Fincantieri has built the world's biggest passenger liner so far, the 109,000 gross tonne Grand Princess.

But he said the continuous fall in prices, now well below those of 1992 while prices for other forms of transport have risen over 40 percent, as well as rising costs have eroded companies' profitability.
